prompt:
This question examines the scalar and vector classification of physical quantities and their kinematic analysis.

(a) State whether each of the following electrical quantities is a scalar or a vector:
(i) Electric potential difference (voltage) [1]
(ii) Electric current [1]
(b) Electric current is depicted on circuit diagrams with arrows indicating direction along connecting wires. Explain why electric current is nevertheless classified as a scalar quantity in basic physics. [1]
(c) A walker travels 120 m due north in a time of 80 s, then turns and walks 50 m due south in a time of 40 s.
(i) Determine the total distance travelled and the magnitude of the resultant displacement from the starting point. [1]
(ii) Calculate the average speed of the walker for the entire 120 s journey. [1]
(iii) Calculate the average velocity of the walker for the entire 120 s journey, stating both its magnitude and direction. [1]

answer.text:
(a)(i) Electric potential difference: scalar.
(a)(ii) Electric current: scalar.
(b) Current does not obey the rules of vector addition (the direction of current is constrained by the wire geometry and cannot be resolved or added using vector triangles/parallelograms independently of the wire; at a junction, currents add algebraically according to conservation of charge, I1 + I2 = I3).
(c)(i) Total distance = 120 + 50 = 170 m. Resultant displacement magnitude = 120 - 50 = 70 m (due north).
(c)(ii) Average speed = total distance / total time = 170 m / 120 s = 1.42 m s^-1.
(c)(iii) Average velocity = resultant displacement / total time = 70 m north / 120 s = 0.583 m s^-1 due north.

(a)(i) Scalar.

(c)(iii) Average velocity = 70 / 120 = 0.583 m s^-1 due north.
